blocks.x: What is the job of the guitar in the band? If you can start on that, why do you think it's good to have one in the band?
Well, the guitar is a rhythm instrument, and it has a tendency to give a dance orchestra some snap. It gives a regular snap, I mean, it's sort of the foundation to an orchestra.
If you were going to only use three rhythms in a band in place of fours, they sometimes use, what three do you think would be best, or would you enjoy working with?
Well, three rhythm, well, I mean, you take bass, drums, and guitar.
Like the old New Orleans bands.
Like the old regular old New Orleans bands. And you just can't beat it for a dance orchestra. When you go into concert work...
You remember that all those years? Yes, indeed.
It'd have to be 50 years.
Yeah. Well, I remember further back than that, you're taking around 1900, I was around 10 years old, is when they had the Golden Rule Band. Now that's the hottest band to my knowledge. Really? Yes.
Who was that band?
Well they was, let's see, they was Mav Franks, he played the piccolo. Jimmy Brown played bass. Oh boy boy boy boy. Al C. Del C. Is he Mav's brother that played?
No, no, no. Al C. Frank.

Al C. Frank played violin. And Steve Wilson had that band. Who was the drummer? Do you remember? I think they had the drummer, do you remember? I think they had the, what was the name of the phone? I think Louis Contra was playing with the band.
Louis Contra was playing with them. I just remember which one of them.

The trombone was a ... Wait a minute. Boy, I got those notes down there.
So I went and checked on the letter.
Yeah, we checked on the letter.
Would it have been a Baptiste, a Leo, by any chance?

That's it. He was a trombone player with them. And oh, I think Tats' daddy was playing trombone. Alexander, yeah. Alexander. He played trombone. Playing trombone. Oh yeah, I thought he was an outdoor player. In the later years he was taking a foul. He played trombone right there. And she was playing, I think Rene Baptiste was playing guitar. And those other creoles, they used to call them a hop band like we call them nowadays. They used to call them a rally band. And those old dignified creoles, wouldn't they let their daughters go when they were going to what Drew was playing?
That band is too ratty.
That band is too ratty. They make them children forget themselves when they get to shake it.
Where did they play? Well they played most everywhere.

But they bought them out of the France Amis Hall. That was strictly dignified. They wouldn't let them play there. And they played the economy, they played the cooperators, which was named the Hopes Hall at that time. And played the Globes Hall. Perseverance maybe? Perseverance.
No, that was another hall they were borrowed from.

They were pretty classic. Yeah, pretty classic. And they were playing out in the economy hall, cooperating in those halls. And the youngsters came home with a ticket, they used to print tickets to the ball then. And they had to go through on that. Them old folks tear their ticket up, they couldn't go there. And those babies were really hot, man. That is the first hot band I can remember. And then in the later years then came the Olympia band. And during that time we had the Superior band, very good band, Imperial, very good band. But they were more on the legitimate side. Very good dance music, but they were more on the legitimate side.
Who was in the Olympic, not everybody, but just one or two to identify?
Well, it was Freddy Kepard, Big Eye Louie, P. Ron, Willie Santiago, and a bass player called Tiet Rochon, he's dead now.
And the Imperial was Manuel Perez.

Manuel Perez, George Fields, Octave Gaspar, and Vic Gaspar. No, no, George Fields, Vic Gaspar was playing with him, George Fields playing, I think O. Gaspar was playing. No, Vic and Oak was playing with John Robichaud. Yeah. Who was the clarinet?
The clarinet, George Baquet.
George Baquet was clarinet. Was it an Olympia band? No, Big Eye Louie?
Yeah.
Big Eye Louie. And it was on bass, there was Jimmy Brown, Tiet Rochon.
I think Jimmy Brown did play with him later. He played with the ladies, yes.

Well, Jimmy Brown was with the Golden Rule until then when they organized the Olympia band, he played with the band, he played with the band, and there was Tiet Rochon, Freddie Capard, Big Eye Louie, Eddie Vinson, trombone, and I see who was playing the drummers. I'm trying to think who was playing the drum with them.
Mac Murray played in any of those bands? No, I don't think Mac.
Mac played with some of those bands.
Cantrell might have been in one.
Yeah, Cantrell. I think Cantrell was playing with Imperial, the band of Perez in that group.
D.D. Chandler, did he play with any of those?
D.D. Chandler, yes, he played, I just remember. I think he played with several of them at a different time.
Wow.
Well, Louie Cantrell was with Robichaud at one time, too.
Now, don't worry about all those exact personnel, there's just a few to identify. A little bit about the Superia.
Yeah, well, Freddie Capard was not the Superia, and Bunk Johnson. There's Bunk Johnson. Who was playing clarinet with them?
There's one picture of the Superia band taken with Keele, not Keele, but Big Eye even in that. Big Eye played.
Yes, well he played with most of the bands.
And they all changed the band.

Yeah, they changed the personnel from time to time. I can remember there was Bunk, Eddie, Eddie Vinson, no no, Eddie Atkins. Eddie Atkins. Bunk, Eddie Atkins. It was Billy Morero, I guess he was manager, wasn't he?
Bill Morero was in the Superior. Yes, he was.
He was playing bass with the Superior. And Willie Santiago, I think Joe Brooks, Joe Brooks was playing with Olympia, too.
Yeah.
Superior. The Superior, because Willie Santiago was playing with Olympia. Joe Brooks was playing with the Superior.
And, uh, I remember the name of Payne, what was his name?
Uh, Richard Payne, he was a guitar player, too. Well, I, uh, I don't remember Richard Payne so well. I saw him once or twice.
He was in a picture, Ronsworth Bunkin, the Superior.
Yes, well, he might have been.
Like we said, they all changed around.
Yes, I remember when Joe Brooks was with him.

Well, nobody much in all this trip is hardly mentioned, Piku. Do you remember when did you hear him? Well, wait a minute, wait a minute. Nobody's been talking about him lately, like Pops Foster, nobody has mentioned him.

He was the clarinet player in the Olympia band when they first started. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he got bigger and a little bit later. I think he went back to the Imperial with Manuel. He was the clarinet player with the Olympia band when they first organized it. And later on he left the band and went with the Imperial. And then George, George Baquet, no, the big guy Louis, went with the Olympia. Then he went with the superiors, and George Baquet went with the Olympia.
Then they went on the road then. Then they went on the road then. Yeah.

So there's one thing about it that Louis, I don't know how he became the lady yet, but Louis wasn't much of a reader. He was a great clarinet player but he was much of a reader. He could spell a little, he would take a number home and work it out. But he was a reader that you could put a piece of music in front of his band and play his thing. And I believe that's why they choose George Baquet, because George Baquet was on the ball. But after George Baquet ditched him in Philadelphia, Louis was the next best man.
Well did you get uptown to hear those bands like Frankie Dooson, and you mentioned Bolton only out at the-

Yeah, well, the Eagle band, I was very familiar with Eagle band. That was Frankie Dooson playing trombone, and Joe Johnson. See Jefferson? Yeah. Well Joe Johnson, man, just on all the Jeppe, the same color, same size and everything. He started trombone.
And very good trumpet.
Well he was not quite as tall as Jefferson. He was about six inches shorter.
But it looked something like him.

And a very good trumpet player. He could make sense of, well Bump played with him at one time too. But when I knew them, they had Joe Johnson on trumpet, Frankie Dooson trombone, Jim Dandy playing bass, Jeff Mumford playing guitar, Henry Zeno playing drum, I wish he could have lived for you to hear him playing drums. Yeah, I've heard of him. He was great. And, uh, I see it was, uh, Daniels on bass, Jeff Mumford on guitar, Sidney Bechet on clarinet.
Do you remember old man Willie Umphrey? That is not our young man.
I know from Jim Umphrey on down. He was called Willie Umphrey.
Did Willie Umphrey play at the Eagle band whenever you heard him or not?
Because he was supposed to play with him for a while. Well, he played with him for a while. But Willie Umphrey was mostly on the road.
That's right.
He loved to travel. And the way he traveled, he played around the world until the circus came to town. And he joined the circus band and took the country with him.
He's still living there. We've got to talk to him.
Yeah, he's been sickly for quite a while.
He's in a wheelchair out of trouble. He's trying to hate to bother him, but someday we'll go out and talk to him.
Yes, indeed. Mm-hmm. Let's see.
Oh, I was going to ask about a couple other uptown trumpet players that nobody seems to know anything much about him, like Edward Clam. Edward Clam.
Well, he was from, I think, Cinderella, La Platt, somewhere out there. Came down the river. Yeah, well, he was sensational. He was a fair. He was a fair kind of player.

And another fellow, Ned. I never heard that's his last name or first name. Do you remember anything about him? Ned. Ned, you see. Came after Bolden and there was some who played maybe a little bit with Frankie Doosman for a while. I don't even hear all those stories. I don't know what's the name.
I don't remember Ned. You don't remember Ned. But I remember Joe Johnson and, oh, who was the other guy?
Was Andrew Kimball very early in the way?

Andrew Kimball, yes. Andrew Kimball was always on the legitimate side though. He was. He was John Robichaud. John Robichaud, yeah. John Robichaud had a band, I'll say, more under the style of Guy Lombardo. Most everything he played was legitimate. It was good dance music but it was on the legitimate side. There was nothing hot about it. And Imperial was pretty much on that order. He played good music, good dance music, but it was not.
Speaking of uptown fellows, what about Lorenzo Stahl? Did he take Brock's place? Was he a little younger than Brock or did he?
Well, yeah, he was younger than Brock. I mean, he'd taken Brock's place.
Oh, do you know that his last name, is it spelled, you know how it's spelled or pronounced exactly, is it Stahl or some people say Star, like the star up in the sky?
No, no, no, it's not like Star in the sky. It's, I think it's S-T-A-W-L-S. Stahls. Stahls.
Somebody said it might have a Z in. That sounds something like the way you said it.

No, no, it's not no Z. No Z. No, not Stahls. It's Stahls. It's T-A-W-L-S. I think that's what it's spelled. I never find it. I looked at it. Yeah, there's a brother out here by the name of Stanley Stahl.
Oh, in Los Angeles.
Yeah. Oh gee, I could stay a month out here and not meet everybody.
No, you're not kidding.
Yeah, Stanley's out here.
Stanley's a bricklayer, but he had another brother by the name of Sidney Stahl, but he died. He was a blast truck. But Stanley's still living, I think, he's still out here.

Yeah, well, Lorenzo was a bricklayer, but he had another brother by the name of Sidney Stahls, but he died. He was a blast truck. But Stanley's still living, I think, he's still out here. Yeah, well, Lorenzo was one of the best guitar players we had uptown.

Was he really a good guitar player? Yeah, he was a good guitar player. Well, you used to sing some of these songs at Fest and I was a little while. Yeah, yeah, yeah, a little while. You think he was mostly an entertainer or he was really a good musician? Yes, he was. A good guitar player.
Yeah, he's a great guy. He was a very good friend of mine. Very good friend of mine. We were like brothers. And where did you live about him? He lived at Leotin and Pitt.
Oh, right out there? Yeah, right out there.
A block above St. Charles and one block below Peters Avenue, which is now Jefferson Davis.
Yeah, Jefferson Davis.
He had a presser by trade. He had a cleaning and pressing establishment.
I was going to ask some more when you were just a small boy. I think one night you were talking about the junk dealers and the old bottle rag man with their tin horns. Were you talking about that?
Yeah, they used to play as much on those tin horns as this guy, how do you call them, the bugle? Bugle Sam.
Yeah, Sam Dine.
They played as much on those tin horns as the bugle Sam played on that bugle. Did he play like the old blues?
Absolutely. Did they do that to sort of advertise that they were coming up the street? That's right, yeah.
Some people know they were the bottle man. If they had any bottles to sell by, they'd get it on and they'd gather their bottles together.
Did they give any other cry along with it? No, no, that's all they used.
That's all they used. Just blowing that horn. They didn't yell out old bottle man. No bottle man, no. That's him with Bugle and Sam, he used to sell waffles. And that was his signal.
There's still another guy down there still does that.
He played the blues on it.
At least two years ago I was.
Yeah. Some of them would just blow a regular army bugle, you know, but Sam used to play the blues.

I was wondering, any church music did you hear? I'm not trying to pry into your affairs. I'm wondering what religion, you were a Methodist, I'm going to get it on to your... Yes. Were you always raised in a Methodist church?

No, I was born and raised Catholic. Oh really? I had my first wife Catholic. We divorced, those Catholics don't divorce you, you know. Yes, that's right. And when I met this wife, well she was Methodist and it's the only way that I could get married again, that by a Methodist preacher, you know, I figured if he was good enough to marry me, he was good enough for me to serve, to attend a subordinary in this church. So I turned Methodist.
There wasn't so much music, I guess, in the Catholic church, it was different there from any other city. No, no. Or worse, just as usual.
It was just a place that naturally caused me to change.
Yes, I mean I wondered the kind of music in the churches when you were young, if you heard anything like the Baptist and Methodist, the spiritual and God's hymn.

Well, I heard most of them because I was a young man, around 18, 20 years old. I used to visit all churches from time to time. I'd go to a Baptist church, I'd go to a Methodist church. I'd go to a Catholic church in the morning, Mass. See, my evenings were always free to go to a church. Sometimes I'd go to, I had some friends of mine who were Baptists, and I had some friends who were Methodists, I'd attend church with them. And I'd tell you from a musical standpoint, well, I prefer the Methodist music and the Catholics.

Well, people like Bud Scott and Mutt Carey, I know, told me years ago, and other people too, they even thought some of the early dance music, the jazz bands, were influenced by the music they heard in the churches.
Well, the Baptist has the same rhythm, and the style of singing is on the blue side.
That's right.
It is. Most Baptists have their singing on the blue side. And they have the perfect rhythm.
Yeah, I like it.
You could dance to it as well as shout to it, you know what I mean?
They really enjoy themselves. Oh, yeah, they do. They do. They'll be happy in church. Well, that's right.
They're supposed to.
What about any parades when you were a boy? I actually heard...

Oh, well, I used to run all the parades, and all the advertisement on the... I was a band that was playing on the corner. I'd be out there. And the parades, and my mother never allowed me to follow the parades. But if they came around the neighborhood I'd follow them a block or two anyway. I used to love the music. Did you ever play, you might as well get that down here too, ever play in any brass bands? Yes. I played one of the two Jaws alto with the, I played one of the two Jaws alto with the, Henry Allen. The old man Henry Allen. The old man Henry Allen.
The old man Henry Allen.
Yes. Yes.
I played one of the one dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear Did you ever play, you might as well get that down here too, ever play in any brass bands?
Yes, I played alto with the Tulane band. I played one or two Jaws alto with Henry Allen.
Oh, the old man Henry Allen.
The old man Henry Allen, yes. I played several funerals and parades with him.
Did you have any instruction on that or pick it up yourself?

Well, David Jones inspired me. He was playing when I got on the board. He was playing alto, playing the what you call a mellophone, yeah. And he played almost as much on his mellophone as Louis Armstrong played on the trumpet. He was just that good at it. He learned how to play sax right on the board.
He hasn't played that before.
He learned how to play sax right on the board. I'm not sure, I believe he got a few lessons from Norman Mason. And he just went right on from there and became one of our best saxophone players.
I know Armstrong gives him credit for helping him with his music too.

Yeah, he was a very good musician. I think he used to play mellophone and he used to play the shell parts. We always had horn parts in the band. But he never used the horn parts. He played the shell parts.
I see how he had read that bass clef and treated it as if it was transposing an E flat instant.
Well, yeah, he told me how he did it. A lot of guys used to wonder how he did it.
There's a trick to that.
Yeah, he played it just as it was. In other words, it was in the bass clef. But he played it as though as in the treble clef.
Yeah, and then on the E flat instrument it comes out right. It comes out right. That's the other one. Yeah, I never thought of that.
Yeah, that's what he did.
He explained it to me.
He said a lot of guys were wondering how I'd do it. He explained to me just how it was. He just played it straight just like he was reading treble clef.
Yeah, pretty good trick.

Uh-huh. And so the people have the Stratford Steamer line, they'd buy, if you were working for them, they'd buy you any instrument you wanted. And they'd save you that cash discount and you'd pay them by the week.
So you told once, on the machine running, how Armstrong got his first horn on the boat. Was it Ori and Hadden?
Yeah, Ori had stood for a horn for him. And he went through paying for it. And when he told Ori he was going on the boat, Ori told him if you go on the boat I'm going
to take my horn.

So he met me at the boat on a rehearsal morning and he said, Pops, I don't believe I can make it. And I said, why? He said, well, I always say if I go on the boat he's going to take my horn. I said, don't worry about the horn, you want to make the trip? I said, you get a horn. He said, yeah, I'd like to make it. I said, will you come on the boat? I said, we'll talk to the captain after rehearsal. So I told Faye about it. He said, you don't have to worry about the horn. He said, Captain will buy him any kind of horn he wants to. So after rehearsal we went to the purchase office on the boat and saw that Captain Roy was there and Faye told him what the situation was. And he said, can a man play? Can he play? Can he play? Faye said, yeah, he can play all right. He said, well you don't worry about the horn, there's something to buy any kind of horn you want. He said, you want to make a trip? You want to go with the boys? He said, yes. He said, we'll buy any kind of horn you want. He said, just be here next Tuesday morning, catch the train, go to St. Louis. Well then you took the train up there. Oh yes, we didn't go on the boat then. Well the first two years, 1918 and 1919, we went up on the train. But from then on we'd wake up and wake back down on the boat. And so when we got to St. Louis, he went to the office, Faye, baby dad's for myself. And Louis went to the office and Faye introduced Louis as the secretary. And he said, so this is Louis Armstrong I've been hearing about. That's him. He said, well Louis, Captain Joe sent a telegram up there and says, well you go out to Huntless Music Store and pick out any kind of horn you want. So you know if he went out to Huntless Music Store and he picked out a Harry B.J. horn. And he got a mouthpiece of things, about five or seven dollars, something like that. Anyway he got the outfit, they could rain around about 72 dollars or something like that.
That story got a lot of old rag and horn and music music. Yes indeed.

Fifteen years ago. And so they kept the boat up in Devonport, Iowa. They had a slew there where they laid the boats up in the winter season. And we went up to pick up the boat that evening and went out, we had supper and we had rehearsal. That night.
What was that?
That was the steamer St. Paul.
St. Paul. And didn't it say good?

Yes. We had rehearsal. So we had rehearsal on St. Paul and Louis liked to do the bell off the horn. And we were playing one number. I don't remember what it was. I should have remembered it. But we were playing one number there and Louis got the plane, he come to an abrupt stop. So face it, what's the matter Louis? He said, man I had to stop and let some of them notes get out of this horn. He was making so many of them. He was hung up in the horn, he couldn't stop and let them get out. So we take the boatman, we work down from Devonport Highway, made every town up down to St. Louis. And then we went to St. Louis for the season. And the band was new to the office personnel, the office was right on the river. And the band was new to the office personnel every day in the season. And we'd leave out in the morning, the whole office crew would come stand on the wall, just listen at the band, and we'd be coming back in the evening and find them there standing just like all the outsiders. They're just new to them every day. I wish I heard that.
Never got used to it.
It was a great band too. One of those bands had something.
I was asking pops up there a little bit about the band that you had. I always had the idea you stayed on the boat and lived there even in St. Louis, but you had a room out there.
No, we had room ears. See that, when I left the boat, they had began to making tramp trips. You had to live on the boat.
Yeah, I mean those kind of trips.

There would be maybe a week in St. Louis and go maybe a week in Devonport Highway and up to St. Paul, Minnesota and work back and further down the river and then all the way back to New Orleans. And I didn't like living on the boat. The first two years we were up there, we were in New Orleans, the season, winter season. And we were in St. Louis, the summer season. See, and we had rooms in town. We'd knock off at night, go to our rooms or go to a restaurant, anywhere we had to go. Well, when they started making those tramp trips, well, you couldn't live off the boat. You had to live on the boat because, I mean, they were...
Yeah, every night sometimes. Yeah. Do you remember in St. Louis any of the places like Tom Turpin and his brother Charlie ran the place Jazzland?
Yeah, we used to go to the Jazzland.
But the theater they had was the Booker T. Washington?
Yeah, Booker T. Washington Theater was on the corner. And right behind it, on Market Street, was the Jazzland.
Yeah. Was the...
Like you said, the theater was on the corner here. And right this house here, back of it, would be the Jazzland. Yeah.

The filling station. I took pictures of where it used to be. There's one place, remember the Rose... Once it was called the Rosebud or Hunting and Shooting Club. It was down on Market Street, a little bit down towards the river.
No, I don't remember.
The Turpin's had a saloon there where Tom used to play piano. Did you ever hear Tom Turpin play piano? No, I never heard him play, no.
He was the famous Ragnarok piano player. They tell me he was a very good piano.
Was the St. Louis District Red Light District over in Chessland, was it still running in those days in 1990?
No, no. They put the damp on Prohibition End. I mean, the damp went on while we went to St. Louis. And I used to go to the chauffeur's club very often.
Well, that was still running when I was in the 1930s and 40s. Yeah.
The other time the guy went broke. When the liquor came in, he put in liquor and he was making lots of money and he started playing fast women and slow horses and broke him.
Do you remember anything about Jazzland, what it was like? Did you ever go there and sit in?

Well, yes. I went there and sit in with the band one night. Turpin had given a macaroni dinner for the Bullock band. And we went on out there. And the guys in the band, at least a piano player in the band, he was rated as the best blues player in St. Louis. I just remember his name. I think his name was John something. And the Russian racket just came out. It was kind of a tough number. So what he done was Pat Foster and I was in the band. Dodge was sitting in the band. And he called Indian Blues. It must have been a made up plot against Pat Foster and I, you see. He called Indian Blues and the band struck the introduction of Russian Rag.
Oh yeah, that's a tough precaution.

We had been playing Russian Rag on the boat for about six weeks, you see. And we missed two measures because we was starting on Indian Blues, you see. But after we played the, we went da da da, da da, da da, da, da, da, da, da. We came right on in, we knew what he was playing.
So they were somewhat disappointed.

We were familiar with the number, we got the number on the boat before they got it. Because Captain Joe, they used to send Captain Joe music by the month. They sent him a stack of music and they'd bill him for it, you see. So we used to get music first. The boats used to get music first. So when the other guys got it, we'd be playing in about three weeks.
What kind of a place was it? Was it a big dance hall?
No, but it was just an open yard.
Oh, jazz? It was outdoors?
Outdoors, yes.
I did hear something about being at Kent there one time, too. Do you remember any Kent over there?

No, not at the time I was there. Not around 1918, 1919. Must have been later. It was just no open yard. And the music stand was on the side. It was covered. It was the only place covered. All the rest was out in the open.

Yeah, I never knew that. Well, I was going to ask a little more about the get back to New Orleans when you were young. One night you mentioned something about was it the bass player didn't show up when you were on the job, you began to play the ...
No, well, no.
When you worked out your bass.

The thing about it is that Jules Batiste, he used the bass very much on the guitar, because they always played small combos. Like the fish fry there was two pieces at the Morris, and the guitar just strumming rhythm was much of a support. That bass gave it more of a sound support. And Jules specialized in the bass. And I adopted that style from him, in fact I had taken lessons from him and I adopted his style of playing. And most of the small jobs, as I said before, Piron used to give me, were just small combos, maybe four pieces. And we used the strongest instrumentation for those four pieces. We used violin, trumpet, and clarinet, and guitar. Well we would use the bass player. See I played enough bass on the guitar to balance the band.
Almost like the piano left hand. Exactly.
That's the general idea.
That's how you worked out that style. That's how you worked out that style.
Almost characteristic in the air.
That's right. That's right. That's right. Yeah.

Sometime we'd use the trumpet and trombone and eliminate the clarinet. That was a good power there. For the dancers still had a good accompaniment with the guitar using the bass. Yeah. Is there any other guitar player that you sort of tried to pattern your style or influence
to more than others that you loved?
Well, I grabbed a few tips from Bud Scott. He's about the only one that I adopted some styles from. The others, they...

I was going to ask, like today, supposedly some kid wants to take up the guitar or banjo and wonders which is which, or if you were going to tell some kids that were getting a band together, which to use, guitar or banjo, which would you advise and why?
Well, I'd advise banjo because it's what the public wants. The music-loving public in a dance orchestra, they like the banjo in preference of guitar. But for myself, I prefer the guitar.
I think the guitar works in a rhythm section better.

It belongs there. It's the first rhythm instrument used in the Dixieland band. Banjo became popular around 1917. That is, down in New Orleans. It had been popular out east. They'd use them quite a bit. But down in New Orleans, the guitar was always the rhythm foundation of the band.

I suppose my kid then is going to get a banjo, takes your advice, and says, well, the public wants that. Would you advise him to get a regular four-string tenor banjo, or would you advise him to get a guitar banjo?

Well, I'd advise to get a tenor because a tenor is easier to find. You can buy a tenor most of the time, but the guitar is kind of a scarce instrument. They're not stocking them anymore. And you'd either have to let Dr. Shushaw and pay about $220. The banjo alone would cost him $180 to have it made in the guitar. And I guess with the case, the case must run him around about $60. The outfit might run around about $225, $230. And you'd have to have it made, especially a lot, that they don't stock them. So I'd advise him to get a tenor banjo.
Oh, and what about the five-string? Is that what's called pector banjo?
No, it's four-string. It's tuned the same as the five-string. It's only, it doesn't have that fifth string.
What's that fifth-string tune for you?
A G.
Is that a higher G or a low G?
No, it's a high G.
Because it's a short string.
Yeah, it's a high G.
That's a string of C, G, D, A.
And G.
And what G is that? The way up higher?
Yeah, it's a...
It's a seven-high?
It's an octave higher than the regular G.
Yeah, octave higher than that G. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. What's the plectrum banjo tuning?
The same with the exception of that fifth string. It's played identically the same as the regulation.
Well, in regard to the instrument yourself, you described the one you made and how you bought this one for $25 in St. Louis.
Yes.
Is that the same one you used in Chicago all those years, the Cook's band and on the Hot Five records?
It's the same one I have right now.
Same instrument you did. And the Jolly Roll Martin records. That's right.
Well, I know I used a guitar on the Jolly Roll Martin records. I have a Martin guitar. Oh, yeah.
And after one you have, what is your guitar now?
It's a Gretsch.
Gretsch. How long have you had that?
That is, it's 1932.
Is there anything about picking a guitar or even what make you prefer, not to return to make any, commit to commercial, and recommend one over the other? Well, no.

I just wanted a few. There's a good guitar as you can play. I played Martin. Martin is a very good guitar. In fact it was the Tops at one time. Fess had one, he said he liked the tone. They're very good. It's a very thin material. Then Fess got a fancy Gibson with the big sound holes like the violin. Yes. No.
But he liked it as well as the old Martin with the round holes. No. The guitars with the hole has a tendency to, how do I put it, throw out the sound more than

those clef holes. You like that round hole. Yeah, round hole. I mean you tested it and it says so too. I don't think about a guitar. Yeah, they are much louder. They have a bigger tone. Yeah bigger tone. I might put it throughout the sound more than those clef holes.
Like that round hole. Yeah, round hole. Tested, but it says so too. I don't think about a guitar.
Yeah, they are much louder.
Have a better tone now. Have a bigger tone.
Yeah, bigger tone, yeah. Broader tone.

Don't worry about making any noise with the saints here because we're just talking. We wanted to sound like home here too. So if you want to do any cooking or anything or talk with, don't sneak around on tiptoes because this is all.
No, you can't disturb nothing. No, we don't care.
I don't want to get a knife in. Yeah. We don't care what sound here.

Yeah, the guitar with the sound hole rather than the clefts, I like better. Now, I like the pat and tail pieces. Of course they get over the sound holes. Had those bridge glued to the ... Oh yeah, you don't like that glued.
I wonder too.
Well I've had a misfortune with them on several occasions.
Yeah, I've been.

It was very damp down the wall. There were times when we had two weeks of rain and I'd pick up my guitar and go on the job with it and the strings would pull the bridge off it. The glue then gets off.

My mother had a guitar and she's a girl and never did anything with it, but my brother and I sort of broke it up when we were kids. We used to play it like a cello and rub the little sticks and it was awesome. We finally broke that thing and snapped off of ours too.
I think Nick Lucas used a guitar with a hole, the sound hole in it. Of course he paid way back there when things were cheap. He paid $325 for his.
That's what I hear, some of those old ones.
And you could hear it cutting through a ten piece band.
Really? Without any electric?
Without any amplifiers. In fact I don't think until today Nick Lucas used an amplifier.
It still doesn't use one.
Still doesn't use one.
What about the size of it? Some of them make them so big you know, that's good or is it?

Well, the dimension of the guitar, so far as the width and length of it, I don't think has as much to do with the sound as the shallowness of it. See, there's two things that will give a guitar, I believe most any wood instrument, a good tone. It's a thin material and shallow.
Not too thick.
Not too deep. Deep tone. Yeah. You get a good shallow guitar and you get a broad tone.
Is there anything special about the strings that you like? Any certain brand or size or material or something?
Well, I like the Gibson string. I think the Gibson has as good a guitar string as any major.

Is that all pretty much, I was thinking about the guitar, I didn't ask intelligent questions on some of these, but are all the strings usually the same, or some of them wild and the top, the highest ones are they just a plain?

Well, they used to have the first three strings, the E, B, and G were steel, all steel. But now you have the rap G, the G is rap as well as the bass strings. And I always use rap G, I like them. Yeah. Yeah. I like the tone of them.
Anything special about your pick or anything?
Well, I use the very blunt pick. I make them out of toothbrush handles. Something real thick.
Something real thick.
Jude used to make his own out of bone. Yeah, not flexible.
No, no, they're not flexible at all.
It's hard. It has a taper on the end.
Yeah.
And it hits just like a finger.
Mm-hmm. Yeah. Solid.
And I can't use those slap picks. I can't keep them straight in my hand. They work this way.
I just can't hold them.
But then I get the other one in between my thumb and these fingers here, see. Yeah. And I can hold it all night.
You're a little bit bigger than some of those little ones? Do you make your picks bigger when you make them, or...? No, I see.
I have one of the answer you use. Yeah, sure.

Mm-hmm. Well, I see. It's only about less and a half an inch wide and just... Mm-hmm. ...about an inch long and tapered. Yeah. And it's almost about three sixteenths of an inch thick. Yeah, it's about. Yeah.
Just depending on the material I had. Sometimes it's a little thicker.
I thought it might be easier to hold it, even make it bigger than that or something, make a big grip.
Well, it would be. It would be. It just depends on, as I said, it depends on the material. This was made of the back of a comb.
Oh, yeah. I see. Yeah.
It was narrow. So I used it just as it was. But it's still, I still get a good grip on it, you see. Oh, yeah, sure. It's between my thumb and these two fingers.
Yeah. First finger then braced against your second finger.
That's right. That's what I use. Mm-hmm. And when you hit, you hit like... That's why the bases ring out, so I hit it solid, you know.
Oh, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
Well, when you first started and you had these people helping you, Jules and others, did you ever get a method book? Never did.
I never began to read music until I got on about 1918.
Then you still didn't get a regular method to start on, I guess?

No, I didn't get a guitar method, I just got a music method. I first got a piano catechism. Yeah. And I learned the notes there, and how to build chords, first, third and fifth. I worked them out on the guitar. And then I bought a guitar method. George, George, Pop Foster, he and I bought a method at the same time. He bought a bass method. It was 1918, when we got in St. Louis. He bought a bass method, and I bought a guitar method. And we went to work on them.
Who was it? You telling us that other guys in the band would be running around at night, but you always...

Yeah, they'd be at either the showbiz club or the jazz lamp. And we'd be in the room wrestling with those books. And I think we didn't understand why we'd have some of the guys in the band, you know, doing intermission. We'd carry out books with us. And the guys would give us the pointers on...
Would you advise young players starting the day to learn to read right away, or to play by ear for a while, or what do you think this has been?
Well, I'd advise them to learn how to read.
Right off?
Right off the reel, yeah. Well, this is an age now that you have to know how to read. You can't get by like we just get by nowadays.
Well, maybe it might be that some of you fellas learned better, I mean, turned out to be the greatest players...
Well, we had better ear training.
Yeah, you had to handle...

Now, I would advise, while learning to read, to practice playing by ear. Because the ear training is the best you can get for dance music. See, the classic music at the time varies so, that it would really be hard to train the ear. You'd have to write music for that. But in playing dance music, ear training is very valuable. It's very valuable. And it gives you a sense of rhythm, a sense of division, a sense of time. Because we played syncopations back in time when I was a youngster. And the musicians, I mean good musicians, couldn't write. They just couldn't get that division. Because they're doing it now, the guys are there writing a thing you can play. And tell you what you play, you do while they're writing it. But at that time, the guys, they were trained in one, or there was a certain rule that they were educated in music by, and that rule held good. And they worked by that rule. And then what we were playing was, they were considered outlaw. See? And it was just a different category than they were taught altogether. And they just couldn't, oh I don't know, just couldn't understand the division, not enough to write it.
And yet they had all those complicated rhythms in there. And they were taught.

Yes. After the guy just developed rhythm of his own, you know what I mean? Just hit him and he had something in him, he just let him give out with it. And if it's just good, well, at least the band tell him to do it again.

I'm wondering, say when you played dances, even after you learned to read or before, whenever you played a lot of pieces, as soon as the leader calls the piece, tells you what key it's in, or maybe they didn't even always tell you what key it's in. Did you start thinking about, I have to play the C card for four measures and I change to F and I go to G and the B flat seven? Well, yes. Those things come in your mind? Yes.
That's right. Well, I never knew the value of measures, but I had a sense of rhythm and I might put it this way, just how far I should go in a certain key.
Did you think now the next card is going to come, I have to change to G or A?
Absolutely.
That was, you didn't just start playing and your fingers find the... No, no.
You had it in here.
You had to be thinking all the time.
Absolutely. Yes, sir. And I'll tell you that I had a sense of harmony, a natural sense of harmony. That's the one thing that made me become so popular.
That's right. Yeah, a lot of people play the wrong chords.
Because, yes, they play a major where a minor should be, or a minor where a major should be, or where I play C, A7, D7, G7. A guy would play, the other guys would play just C and G7.
Simplified, doesn't it? Yes, I know. It doesn't always harmonize. Two cards.

But I always tried to find chords that would harmonize. And try to find as many changes that would harmonize with the number as possible. I always had that natural sense of harmony. And that's the one thing that made me very popular as a guitar player. Because guys had been playing with the very, guys that were supposed to be famous in those days, Joe Brooks and Rene Baptiste. And those people, when I played the number I found so many changes in between what they played, that the guys wondered how I played it and didn't read. I just had a natural sense of harmony, I could feel it. And at one time I could modulate. You see now the bands play a number and they change keys, they just jump down from one key to the other. But in those days we used to modulate to the key. You modulate about four meshes or eight meshes into the next key, working to gradually. And I used to modulate from any key.
From C to A flat.

See guys playing the number and C and he want to fall to A flat, he just drop down in A flat with both feet. See he ain't got the courtesy enough to modulate. It's much smoother when you. Oh yeah, when you just work into it.
They're double measures, number three. That's right.
And man, I used to make chords and just work right in the front seat, work right on into A flat. See. I'm rusty on that now because the bands doesn't do it anymore. See.

But at one time you've written all those out, I mean the B, A flat, C, and you've actually written out on paper, not the actual notes, but I mean your succession of chords. Yes, uh-huh, succession of chords. You really thought that in your mind. Absolutely, that was in here. And your fingers didn't just start to go along. No, no, no. You're thinking about something else.
No, no, that was in the mind. Yes, yeah. A little mind.

Because I was asking for instance, Ed Garland, in playing his bass, in which he doesn't have the same problem quite as you playing the chords. No. But they do play chords on the bass too, you know. Oh yes. And I asked him if he was conscious of the chords as he played them and he said no, hardly ever. He said I could be talking to somebody. And he'd be playing his bass and yet his fingers would find the right chords on any piece that he knew. He never, as he knew a piece, he never thought of what chord he or even what key it was in.
Well, I, there's lots of guys can do that.
I never could.
You always actually thought of what I'm doing.
I'm always conscious of what I'm doing. How's the thing you had on the guitar with all those strings?
I have, have you ever heard young Linus McLean play the guitar? Yes, not very much.
Not very much.
Well he's another Les Paul, believe me. I've heard him really, really stick out.
Heard his father a lot more on bass, but you say his father was a guitar player.
Yes, he's a guitar player, along in my class. But Linus, I mean, put both of us in the sewer.
Linus is great. As far as that type of thing.

He's a guitar player, he has, and a single note technician. And I've heard he's not very much as a chord man in a band. But man, he has technique on the single note man. And he makes chords so far as the number he's playing it goes. But I mean for a rhythm man in a band, he's not much a rhythm man. Because he knows chords. He can take any part in an orchestration. And he'd play it on the guitar, trombone, clarinet, anybody's part. He'd play it on the guitar.
What do you think is the main job of the guitar in a band?
Rhythm.
Rhythm.

Now okay, a guitar is entitled to a soloist, well as nobody else in a band. If he's a soloist, and Ernest is one, I'll tell you what, if I was able to have a band, I would like to have Ernest as a first guitarist. All I want to do is play rhythm. But I want to feature him on solo. Circus solo. For St. Joe.

To get back to your rhythm guitar, one of those are our banjo. There was a banjo player who came over here from England last year. Nice enough guy and knew the instruments fairly well. But he was always going plenka, plenka, plenka, plenka back and forth always a double stroke. Yes, yes. Well, usually do you just hit thumb the down stroke? Of course you have that more different style in your guitar. Yeah. That bass.
The down stroke, that down stroke is rhythm.
But you don't try to always snap back?

No, no, no. Because many of the double strokes. Now and then you'll hit a double stroke. For instance we'll say on, the way we used to use, used to add lead, even on the rhythm instrument, was on the last course what we call the hot chorus. All the instruments play as they should. The rhythm, play rhythm straight up. Now on the hot chorus everybody gets cut loose on that last chorus you see. Everybody's at liberty. The bass player, now you see like these bass players all night long, four beats to the bass, boom boom boom boom boom boom boom boom. That's not bass for the Dixieland. Solid. One, two, one, two, one, two. When it's not in. Do do do do do do do do do do do. Do do do do do. Do do do do. Do do do. Do do do. Do do do. Do do. Do do. One. That's bass.
That's bass.

That's bass for the dance orchestra. Now in the last chorus, everybody gets a window, you see. Then you get . You see everybody's at liberty in that last chorus, you're getting hot. But throughout the number, up until that last chorus, bass player is supposed to play first and third. Now the same with the drummer. Hell, four beats on the bass drum, man. That's all right for that last chorus. The bass drum is supposed to play the same as the bass. One, two, one, two, one, two. Whatever you do with the sticks on the snare drum, that bass is supposed to be . Now in that last chorus you want to get hot, that's the hot chorus. But you can't tell the youngsters that nowadays. You tell the bass player, play one, two, man. He says, man, some people come up here and they think I can't play no bass. That's their attitude, you see. Drummers likewise. And they all want to be Dixieland players. I mean they're not playing Dixieland.
They're not playing Dixieland.

Even Buddy. Of course Buddy don't date back with me. Buddy, because he's a latecomer. He's a latecomer. See, but Buddy's the same way. Man I was racing him and Mike here, and I was trying to get him to play the type of bass, you know what I mean? And he gets to play and he goes, that four, four beat, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Running all up and down the neck of the bass. Yeah, you see. Yeah.
Which is it. I think it looks good, but it doesn't get to be a band of the right support. No musician can't appreciate it.

There's somebody out there that knows what it's all about, they think he's racing sand, you know what I mean? Yeah. But I know better than you know better. See? And I tell him, he wouldn't tell me he didn't want to do it, but I can see his attitude, he become indignant, you know, about that. He's going, I'll catch it, I'll catch it, just go, I don't want that. If I'm rehearsing a band, let a man play like a talent, if I go ahead and play he'll catch it. You know what I'm telling me Bill? That's why I've never had no band. And see because if I'm going to rehearse a band, I mean play it the way I ask you to play. And any musician can do it. If you can play it all, you can play it. If you can play it double four beats, you can play it too. It's hard to be easy.
Absolutely.

But those guys are afraid of criticism. Afraid they go somewhere and play like that, somebody's just going to come in and say they can't play. Well I'm not worrying about what the musician said because he doesn't mean anything to the band. Nine out of ten he comes in free. And when he gets in there he don't spend anything, he only comes there to criticize. You see what I mean? That's all he comes there to criticize. Either constructive or destructive, either one. If you're good he'll praise you, and if you're bad he'll talk about you.
But they're not the ones that support the band.

They're not the ones that support the band. They want to play. I'm playing for these people and I'm spending their money keeping their house open and paying my salary. And let's remember what the musicians are going to say about it. Eventually they will realize that the band can play. Maybe they'll not play to the first night to come in there. But if they keep coming, they'll eventually realize the band can play. You don't have to worry about that. Absolutely. You don't have to worry about it. But that's the trouble with the musician of today. I say even the older ones, Buddy is not an old musician, but he's an old man in the dance, in the music world. Before he played he's been going around to dances, and he ain't good bands, and he knows about good music. But they have that inferiority complex, afraid the other fellow will criticize them, they can't play. I still play the same way I played 40 years ago. And the people still like it.
It still sounds good to me and the people are still crazy about it. They'll give you a chance to hear you. That's right. They'll give you a chance to all through them at the end.
Oh, what? I mean, I have one style of playing, and it has made me very popular. Yeah, but it was good then.
That's right.
It's made me very popular.
No state.

I mean, I've seen names travel all over the world. As I say I've got correspondence here from Australia, Canada, Europe, Italy, France, Switzerland. I mean, the people I've never seen, they've never seen me. They only heard some of the records I worked on. And my playing attracted them to the extent where they wanted to correspond with me. So I mean, there must be something to it.
That's right.
So why should I worry about another musician criticizing what I do?

Trying to keep up with the label style like that. Well, I was going to ask, in regard to the New Orleans style of music, to me there's always a distinct style, because I was raised otherwise and started in classical music and heard bands up north. And to me there's a definite New Orleans style. What is it, would you say, that makes the music different down there than other places? Or if you can pin it down, I don't know if you can. I mean, what would you say is really typical that makes a New Orleans band sound New Orleans?

Well, I'll tell you, for one thing, it's originality. When the bands in New Orleans played like New Orleans band, they didn't try to copy no late style or no new band that came to town, while they could appreciate the difference, the variety, but they didn't try, they had their own style and they stuck with it. And they were all together on it. Everybody felt the same way. Then the next.

So from then on I used to always challenge him to play pool. Either one of us couldn't play. And we used to get a kick out of playing each other. In fact that's what I felt. And so from then on I'd never asked him to play pool. He must have felt something was wrong. He never asked me and I never asked him to play pool.
Then what happened is that night that all of us would be through here until I met him. Get that finish up. Yeah so Butchie.
After Butchie told me he didn't want me to say nothing to him and Joe told me, well what are you going to do Butchie? I'm not going to do anything. He said man, I'm a bad guy.

The same way, then the next thing about it, there was no dissension in the band. Everybody was happy. Just one big family. When they played the job, everybody was glad to play the job. They loved music, and they loved each other. They liked to play together. And they had one distinct style of putting over their music. They rehearsed the number. If the number was written slow, they'd play it as it was written. And if it didn't sound good to the band in that slow tempo, they'd pick up the tempo. And if it sounded better in the fastest tempo, that's the way they played it.
A friend and I were talking the other day, it looks like the New Orleans fellows are about the only ones that can always pick the right tempo, it seems. I mean, they always know just whether-

Well, that they had. See, they, they, they, the fact that they were outlaw made them good. Because you'll find, I've experienced it with Charlie Cook's band. Charlie Cook has put numbers out for rehearsal. And the guys didn't like the number when they played it over the first time. And they made such a poor effort in playing the number that Charlie got disgusted and he put the number aside. He said, oh, we'll put this aside. Maybe later on we'll play it later. And maybe about three nights after, some guy come back and he'd come to work and I'd say, man, you remember that number we were playing the other day that you put back? Charlie Cook said, man, Horace Hyde played that number.
Man, you should, yeah, man, that number's good. You know what I mean? Well, those things.
Well, Charlie Hyde made the number good. See? The number was no better when Charlie Hyde got a lesser or-
The same number.

The same number. They got the same time we did. But they worked on it and made something out of it, see? They might have changed the arrangement a little. They might have changed the rhythm. But it appealed to them when they heard it on the radio. But when he was trying to play it, it didn't appeal to them at all. They wouldn't even make a good effort to try to make something out of them. And that's the thing we used to do. We'd get a number and some of the guys would say, oh man, that's good. The hell ain't no good. They said, well, let's play it over. Let's make it good. Maybe the tempo's too slow or maybe it's too fast. Let's take the slow tempo and see what we can do with it, see? Well, they get to working on the numbers and some guy get an idea and, you know, he's injected into the numbers, you know, it's not on the music. But he gets out and thinks something sounds good and he turns loose with it. I said, well, that's good, man. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again. Let's try it over again.
The trombone feature?
No, it didn't matter. That rhythm stood. The standard rhythm.
The rhythm was pretty solid.
Solid. That's right.

I was wondering if people have said to me too that they've noticed the New Orleans bands, or in general I'd say that you can put it that way, the colored bands play so much better together, and sometimes you think maybe the guys get along better together, or happier working together than some of the bands.
Well, there was one thing about it. They were very good.
He said, I told him, come around sometime, time out, a few lessons. So, Louis started to teach him.
Paul Dufresha He played everything in the background.
Seems like I heard it one time, they had music there too.

Well, it was a nightclub at one time. Oh, it really was. Yeah, it was a nightclub at one time. Dufresha had it as a gambling place when it first started. Called it B-25. Yeah. And the fellow named Paul Dufresha had it. It was a gambling place. And the Lord got closing up these gambling houses. And he made a nightclub out of it.
Yeah.

Well, that died down pretty soon. And he started closing up nightclubs. Yeah. When he closed nightclubs, he opened up gambling houses again. Because it was always against the law, you know. Oh, sure. He paid off the nightclub. He was paying to pay off there. He operated there for years. I don't know. Is he still gambling there?
No, he tore it down.
What?

What? Yeah, that's about the time you moved. The same year, because when I moved down there in 1956, it was torn down. Yes, indeed. And they tore down in 1955, probably within a few weeks or months after you left.
That's the last time, yes.

Oh, yeah, that was gone to the time I moved down about a year after you left. Yes, yes. And the time I got there, it was gone. Nothing there. But they did have gambling, I understand, up there until I was never in the place. But they had gambling, I guess, until the end. Yeah, I guess so.

Yeah, because Paul Dufresher, of course, he died. He was the only gamekeeper down there. I don't know if he did anything with his money. He bought several pieces of property there. Oh, it'll fill after you. Yeah. So that's extremely well fixed. The rest of them, they made a whole lot of money and they spent it just like they made it big time.

Well, there's just one little corner there of the old district that's left the place, around the corner where Lula's had a saloon. I guess it was a bar room next to Lula. Yes. That building's still there. I see. And then the one back, a couple little crib places. And then the one at the corner, somebody told me Tony Jackson used to play.
Yes.
There was Franklin and the Edmonds.
Yeah.
That building's still there, everything else is there. Even all the buildings around there. The town has really been chanted.
Yes.
Rampart Street has been in the little neutral ground, the place of being a big garden. They put it down about six feet higher.
Yes, they cut out of trees from it, put you to far left there.
Yeah, cut down all the trees. There was a big highway that goes through where Basin Street is now, up to the City Hall and all that. Have you seen the new City Hall? I guess not.
No, I saw there's simply a postcard of it. It's right there on the Dio.
It's beautiful building. Remember where the Funky Butt Hall used to be?
Yes.
The City Hall sits on all that character. When Louis was raised, all those on Liberty Street, all that just to be vacant lots or else the City Hall and building a big library.
Yeah, they changed that town a lot. Oh, yeah. You saw the Union Station. Transformation.
Well, the rest of the town, they saw them modern life that day.
They had completed landscape in front of it when I left.
They saw them now. They got a big statue up there or somebody.
Is it Clayborne? I don't know.
Either Ivorville or Bienville or somebody. Yeah, it was one of those. I think one of the guys that discovered or founded New Orleans.
Governor Claiborne was, he was governing Russia. There were three brothers on the streets with AMAP, the Claiborne, Bienville, and Ivorville.
Well, I think Claiborne was later. They gave us the first American governor when he came to.
That's right.
